summary: Sirach 46 praises Joshua, Caleb, the judges, and Samuel as part of the book’s procession of Israel’s honored ancestors. The chapter moves from Joshua’s victories and Caleb’s endurance to a brief blessing on the judges, then gives Samuel the longest attention as prophet, judge, kingmaker, and witness even after death.
whyItMatters: This chapter shows how Sirach uses remembered leaders to teach faithful conduct: courage, persistence, refusal to turn away, and public integrity. It also shows the book reading Israel’s past as moral formation, not only as history retold.

context.author: Yeshua son of Eleazar son of Sira, a Jerusalem teacher and scribe; his unnamed grandson later translated the Hebrew book into Greek in Egypt.
context.audience: Students seeking disciplined wisdom in Jerusalem, and later Greek-reading Jews in Egypt or the wider diaspora.
context.date: The Hebrew work was composed in the early second century BC and was likely complete around 180–175 BC. The grandson arrived in Egypt around 132 BC and translated it during his stay.
context.setting: Jerusalem under Hellenistic rule, with temple worship, ancestral law, scribal study, and Greek-speaking Mediterranean culture all in view.
context.literaryForm: Wisdom instruction that includes poetic teaching, maxims, hymns, prayer, and praise of Israel’s ancestors.

outline.heading: Joshua, successor and warrior
outline.note: Joshua is praised as Moses’ successor, Israel’s deliverer in battle, and one who called on the Most High when surrounded by enemies.

outline.heading: Caleb preserved for inheritance
outline.note: Joshua and Caleb are remembered for resisting the people’s sinful complaint, while Caleb’s old-age strength becomes a sign that following the Lord is good.

outline.heading: The judges blessed by name
outline.note: The judges are honored as those who did not turn away from the Lord, with a blessing that their memory and name be renewed.

outline.heading: Samuel’s faithful authority
outline.note: Samuel is presented as prophet, judge, and maker of kings, whose prayer is answered when the Lord thunders from heaven.

outline.heading: Samuel’s testimony and final prophecy
outline.note: Before death Samuel testifies to his innocence, and after death he is portrayed as still speaking prophetically to the king.

keyVerses.text: Joshua the son of Nun was valiant in war, and was the successor of Moses in prophecies. He was made great according to his name for the saving of God’s elect, to take vengeance on the enemies that rose up against them, that he might give Israel their inheritance.
keyVerses.why: This opening names Joshua’s role in the chapter: successor, warrior, and agent in Israel’s inheritance.

keyVerses.text: that all the children of Israel might see that it is good to follow the Lord.
keyVerses.why: This line states the lesson drawn from Caleb’s preserved strength and inheritance.

keyVerses.text: Samuel, the prophet of the Lord, loved by his Lord, established a kingdom and anointed princes over his people.
keyVerses.why: The verse introduces Samuel’s section and gathers the major roles Sirach highlights: prophet, beloved servant, and kingmaker.

keyVerses.text: Before the time of his age-long sleep, he testified in the sight of the lord and his anointed, “I have not taken any man’s goods, so much as a sandal;” and no one accused him.
keyVerses.why: Samuel’s integrity is summarized through his public testimony and the absence of accusation.

questions.question: Why does the chapter begin with Joshua?
questions.answer: Sirach is in a section praising Israel’s ancestors, and Joshua follows Moses as his successor. The chapter presents him as valiant in war, connected to prophecy, and instrumental in bringing Israel into its inheritance.

questions.question: What does “successor of Moses in prophecies” mean here?
questions.answer: The chapter says Joshua succeeded Moses and links that succession with prophecies, but it does not explain the phrase in detail. A cautious reading is that Sirach presents Joshua as continuing Moses’ divinely guided leadership, without spelling out a separate theory of prophecy.

questions.question: Why does Sirach mention the sun going back?
questions.answer: The line points to Joshua’s battle memory, where an extraordinary day is associated with Joshua’s hand. Sirach’s purpose here is praise: Joshua is portrayed as a leader whose victory displayed divine help.

questions.question: Does this chapter approve of all the violence it describes?
questions.answer: The chapter celebrates Joshua’s victories, including his sword against the cities and the destruction of those who resisted. It treats these events as the saving of Israel and the giving of its inheritance under divine aid. That positive portrayal is explicit, but the poem does not consider the conquered peoples’ experience or give a general rule approving every war.

questions.question: Why are Caleb and Joshua paired together?
questions.answer: Sirach says that in the time of Moses they withstood the adversary, hindered the people from sin, and quieted wicked complaining. They are also singled out from six hundred thousand people on foot as the two preserved to enter the inheritance.

questions.question: What is the point of Caleb’s old age?
questions.answer: The chapter says the Lord gave Caleb strength and that it remained with him to his old age. That endurance leads to his entry into the hill country and becomes an example so Israel can see that it is good to follow the Lord.

questions.question: Why are the judges mentioned so briefly?
questions.answer: Sirach gives the judges only a short collective blessing rather than retelling their stories one by one. The focus is on those whose hearts did not turn away from the Lord and on the renewal of their honored name among their children.

questions.question: What roles does Samuel have in this chapter?
questions.answer: Samuel is called the prophet of the Lord and is said to have established a kingdom and anointed princes. He also judges the congregation by the law of the Lord, calls on the Lord during conflict, and testifies publicly to his own integrity.

questions.question: What does it mean that Samuel prophesied after he fell asleep?
questions.answer: “Fell asleep” refers to Samuel’s death. The verse recalls the episode in 1 Samuel 28 in which Samuel announces Saul’s approaching defeat and death after Saul seeks him through a medium. Sirach treats that speech from the earth as a final example of Samuel’s prophetic witness, without retelling the circumstances of Saul’s forbidden consultation.

glossary.def: The land and future given to Israel in the chapter’s memory of Joshua and Caleb.
A title for God used when Joshua calls for help while enemies press around him.
A divine title used for God in the accounts of Joshua’s and Samuel’s prayers.
Earlier leaders of Israel whom the chapter blesses collectively for not turning away from the Lord.
The chapter’s phrase for Samuel’s death before it describes his final prophetic witness.
